name: Self-tanning mousse
lead: Self-tanning mousse is a foam-format sunless tanning product, usually applied with a mitt, that colours the skin through a sugar-derived color additive called dihydroxyacetone (DHA). Other sunless tanners come as lotions, gels, sprays, wipes and drops. [1][2]

DHA reacts with amino acids in the dead cells of the outermost skin layer to form brown pigments called melanoidins, a Maillard-type reaction. The colour develops over hours and fades over about a week as the surface skin sheds. The process does not involve melanin or UV radiation. [1][3][4]

Dermatology reviews state that DHA has a generally favourable topical safety record, that sunless tanners regulated as cosmetics provide minimal to no photoprotection, and that safety of inhalation and mucous-membrane exposure (as in spray booths) warrants further study. Studies of sunless tanning as a substitute for UV exposure have produced mixed behavioural findings. [2][5][6]
infobox: Cosmetic; DHA approved as external-use color additive

paras: Mousses are whipped, foam-textured sunless tanners. A patent family dating from 2000 describes a self-tanning mousse composed of a self-tanning agent with a nitrogen-free polymer and nitrogen-free surfactant in a cosmetically acceptable carrier. [7][8]

According to Grokipedia, DHA concentrations in sunless tanners typically range from about 1 to 15 percent, the colour develops within roughly 2 to 4 hours and lasts 3 to 7 days; these figures come from an AI-generated source. [1]

DHA is a three-carbon sugar. Reviews describe it as acting only on the surface of the skin, in the stratum corneum, rather than stimulating the melanin-producing tanning pathway that UV radiation activates through the melanocortin 1 receptor and MITF. [1][3][9][10]

Because the colour depends on skin amino acids and DHA concentration, a Thai study of three DHA creams at 3.5, 4.2 and 5 percent found that colour matching required higher concentrations in darker-skinned volunteers. [11]

Grokipedia credits the discovery of DHA's skin-colouring effect to biochemist Eva Wittgenstein in the 1950s, the launch of the first self-tanning lotion, Man-Tan, in 1959, and FDA approval of DHA as an external color additive in 1977. These dates have not been independently verified here. [1]
No trial has focused specifically on mousse formulations as opposed to DHA tanners in general. Human studies of DHA and sunless tanning cover behavioural prevention, safety and camouflage uses.

subs.h: Sunless tanning as a substitute for UV exposure
paras: A randomized trial of 250 women on Massachusetts beaches tested a skin cancer prevention intervention that promoted sunless tanning as a substitute for sunbathing. [12] A separate randomized trial examined how UV photographs, photoaging information and use of sunless tanning lotion affected sun protection behaviours. [13] A nationwide representative survey examined users of sunless tanning products and noted a concern that such products may lead people to overestimate their natural skin type and take riskier tanning decisions. [14]
Reviews report minimal to no photoprotection from DHA; a 2023 randomized trial reported protection against visible light by DHA in people with erythropoietic protoporphyria. [5][15]

The FDA regulates sunless tanners as cosmetics, allows DHA for external use and advises avoiding ingestion, inhalation and contact with eyes, lips and mucous membranes. Spray booth and airbrush application are not approved uses according to a 2018 review. [2][5]

A 2023 review reported irritant and allergic contact dermatitis from DHA, and in-vitro changes in cell function at low millimolar concentrations, while noting that concentrations far higher than those in products were needed for cytotoxicity. [5] Because UV photoprotection is not provided, products do not replace sunscreen. [2][5]
In appearance communities, self-tanning mousse is one of the common UV-free ways to adopt a tanned look. Application tools such as a tanning mitt are used with it.

timeline.event: Grokipedia reports the launch of the first DHA self-tanning lotion, Man-Tan. [1]
Grokipedia reports FDA approval of DHA as an external-use color additive. [1]
Patent applications describe a self-tanning mousse composition. [7][8]
A review of DHA properties and safety is published in Photodermatology, Photoimmunology & Photomedicine. [5]
